title: VCP
teaches: The VCP (volatility contraction pattern) as we trade it: a leader in an uptrend pulls back in a run of swings that each get smaller, volume dries up into the tight final swing, the pivot is the high of that final swing, the buy is the trade through it at market in regular hours and no more than 4% past it, the stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap

facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.
facts.claim: We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA: too stretched to buy.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: Later sells are a judgment too: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.
facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: In a Red market: mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
facts.claim: D46: in a Red market, mostly cash.

facts.quote: Never take a trade from an alert, a post or a video without your own entry, stop and size by these rules.
facts.claim: F66: never take a trade from an alert, a post or a video without your own entry, stop and size.

facts.quote: No setup, no trade: never force a trade to have something on; cash is a position.
facts.claim: D44: no setup, no trade; cash is a position.

facts.quote: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
facts.claim: D39: entry, stop and size written down before the open.

facts.quote: I want to see the stock move from greater volatility on the left side of the price base to lesser volatility on the right side.
facts.claim: Minervini: volatility should fall from the left side of the base to the right.

facts.quote: As a rule of thumb, I like to see each successive contraction contained to about half (plus or minus a reasonable amount) of the previous pullback or contraction.
facts.claim: Minervini: each contraction about half of the one before, give or take.

facts.quote: The progressive reduction in price volatility, which will be accompanied by a reduction in volume at particular points, eventually signifies that the base has been completed.
facts.claim: Minervini: shrinking swings and falling volume at points signal a finished base.

facts.quote: a flat base structure that is four to seven weeks in duration. With this type of base, there is no real volatility contraction as it remains a tight and narrow pattern or box
facts.claim: Minervini: a four-to-seven-week flat base is a box with no real volatility contraction.

facts.quote: from a 25 percent correction, to a 10 percent, to a 5 percent, and so forth, which would be indicative of a classic VCP progression.
facts.claim: Minervini: 25 percent, then 10, then 5 is a classic VCP progression.

facts.quote: I never go against the long-term trend. I look to go long a stage 2 uptrend and go short a stage 4 downtrend, plain and simple.
facts.claim: Minervini: long only in a Stage 2 uptrend.

facts.quote: If you're too late, you run the risk of buying a late-stage base that is obvious to everyone and prone to failure.
facts.claim: Minervini: a late-stage base is obvious to everyone and prone to failure.

facts.quote: To time my entry, I look for price consolidations, which are momentary pauses or periods of rest within the context of a prior uptrend.
facts.claim: Minervini: the consolidation is a pause inside a prior uptrend.

facts.quote: Lack of volume however, does raise a red flag; volume would need to come in soon after. As always, maintain your stop regardless.
facts.claim: Minervini: light breakout volume is a red flag; keep the stop regardless.

facts.quote: The pivot is the top of the final contraction. Not the highest price of the entire base, but the level the final tight consolidation keeps running into.
facts.claim: ChartMill: the pivot is the top of the final contraction, not the base's highest price.

facts.quote: The final contraction is the most important one. It has to be tight: ideally under 10%, and the closer to 3% to 6%, the better.
facts.claim: ChartMill: the final contraction must be tight, ideally under 10%, best 3% to 6%.

facts.quote: If you see several down days on heavy volume in the right half of the base, there is still distribution going on in the stock and you are too early.
facts.claim: ChartMill: several heavy down days in the right half mean distribution; you are too early.

facts.quote: A first or second base after the start of a new uptrend has better odds than a third or fourth.
facts.claim: ChartMill: a first or second base has better odds than a third or fourth.

facts.quote: In a negative market environment, even perfect VCPs fail en masse, simply because there aren't enough buyers to carry breakouts through.
facts.claim: ChartMill: in a negative market even perfect VCPs fail en masse.

facts.quote: An orderly pullback and consolidation with higher lows and tightening range in the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: an orderly consolidation with higher lows and a tightening range.

facts.quote: The pivot is the high of the final contraction. It may sit below the base's left-side high.
facts.claim: The pivot is the high of the final contraction; it may sit below the base's high.

facts.quote: The first (deepest) contraction is 10% to 40%. Never a base that fell 60% or more.
facts.claim: The first contraction is 10% to 40%; never a base that fell 60% or more.

facts.quote: The final contraction is 10% or less; 3% to 6% with tight closes is best, 8% to 10% with loose closes is B-.
facts.claim: The final contraction is 10% or less; 3% to 6% with tight closes is best.

facts.quote: Higher lows: the final contraction's low is above the lowest low of the base.
facts.claim: The final contraction's low is above the base's lowest low.

facts.quote: Volume dries up: the final contraction's average daily volume is below the first contraction's and below the 50-day average, with at least one day in the final contraction at or under half the 50-day average.
facts.claim: Volume dries up into the final contraction.

facts.quote: No selling on the right side: no down day in the second half of the base on volume of 1.5 times the 50-day average or more.
facts.claim: No heavy down day in the second half of the base.

facts.quote: A grade cue: a pivot at or near a 52-week or all-time high (no overhead supply) is A+; a pivot well below the left-side high is B-.
facts.claim: A grade cue: a pivot near a 52-week or all-time high is A+.

facts.claim: A grade cue: a shakeout of a nearby low that recovers, then a higher low.

facts.claim: Three or four clean contractions, each about half the last, is the A+ picture.

facts.claim: A first contraction over 40%, or a fall of 60% or more, ends it.

facts.claim: A close below the final contraction's low restarts the count.

facts.claim: A heavy-volume down day in the right half ends it before the buy.

facts.claim: Price more than 4% above the pivot when you find it is a skip.

facts.quote: After the buy: a breakout day that closes back inside the base (the squat) is the warning with the worst numbers in the scan, not an exit by itself.

facts.claim: Warnings, not exits: a close under the 20-day soon after, three lower lows on rising volume.

facts.claim: Best as a first or second base; a third or fourth base late in a long run is a mistake.

facts.claim: One full buy at one price, one stop. No pilot buys, no adding.

questions.q: What does a VCP stand for?
choices: Volatility Contraction Pattern
Velocity Confirmation Pattern
Volume Compression Pattern
Volatile Continuation Pattern
questions.answer: Volatility Contraction Pattern
questions.why: Volatility Contraction Pattern. The name is about price swings that contract. A sideways wiggle whose contractions do not shrink is not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: VCP stands for volatility contraction pattern. The swings in the base contract.

wrong.Volume Compression Pattern: Volume matters, but the name is about the size of the price swings.
wrong.Velocity Confirmation Pattern: That is not the name. A VCP is named for price swings that contract.
wrong.Volatile Continuation Pattern: The name says contraction, not continuation. It is named for swings that shrink.

questions.simple: The name is Volatility Contraction Pattern, as the price swings in the base contract more and more.

reasons: the name is quoted from the ChartMill guide; the Minervini archive pages could not be reopened in this pass

questions.q: In this chart, the pullbacks inside the base get smaller from the left side to the right.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Each dip meets fewer sellers, so each pullback is smaller. Minervini says swings are biggest when sellers rush to take profits and shrink as sellers become scarcer. That is why a tightening base is ready, and swings that do not shrink are not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: Each dip meets fewer sellers, so the swings shrink from left to right.
questions.simple: True. Each dip meets fewer sellers, so each pullback is smaller, and that makes the base ready.

reasons: Minervini page is an archive capture that could not be reopened in this pass

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Each pullback in a VCP is ___ than the one before it.
questions.answer: smaller
questions.why: Smaller. Each successive pullback in a VCP is smaller than the one before. A wiggle that does not shrink is not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: Every pullback in a VCP is smaller than the last.

questions.q: Where is this VCP's pivot, the level it must trade through?
choices: The low of the first pullback
The close before the breakout
The high of the final contraction
The highest price in the base
questions.answer: The high of the final contraction
questions.why: The high of the final contraction. It is the level the last tight swing keeps running into, so trading through it means buyers have cleared the last supply. It is not the highest price of the whole base: on this chart the last swing's high sits under that peak.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the top of the last, tightest swing.

wrong.The highest price in the base: The pivot may sit below the base's high. The last swing's high is the level to clear.
wrong.The low of the first pullback: That is the bottom of the deepest swing, far from the breakout level.
wrong.The close before the breakout: The pivot is a price level set by the base, the high of the final contraction, not one day's close.

questions.simple: The pivot is the high of the final, tightest swing. Trading through it means the last supply is cleared.

reasons: the pivot is a proposed card criterion, not an owner ruling

questions.story: The day before a breakout.

questions.q: A VCP's pivot may sit below the highest high of the base.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The pivot is the high of the final contraction, and it may sit below the base's left-side high. ChartMill says the same: it is not the highest price of the entire base. A pivot well below the left-side high does grade B-, so it is a weaker location, but it is still the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the last swing's high, even when the base high is higher.
questions.simple: True, because the pivot is the high of the last swing, and that can sit below the highest price in the base.

reasons: pivot and its grade cue are proposed card criteria

questions.q: The buy is a market order, placed once price trades through the pivot in regular hours.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We buy at market as price trades through the pivot, and only in regular hours. A resting limit order can sit unfilled while the stock runs, and then you chase it past our 4% limit. At market you get the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Trade through the pivot, regular hours, market order.
questions.simple: True. We buy at market once price trades through the pivot, in regular hours, because a resting limit can miss the move.

deeper.counter: Some guides tell you to place a buy stop-limit order just above the pivot with your broker. Our rulebook says something different: entries are market orders, placed in regular hours once price trades through the pivot.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 market orders, E58 regular hours)

questions.q: On this VCP breakout, which is our primary stop?
choices: Exactly on the day's low
At the 50-day average
At the low of the first pullback
A few cents under the day's low
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the day's low. If price comes back through the day's low, the breakout has failed, and the loss is known before the buy. The stop sits a few cents under it, not exactly on it, and the size comes from this stop. The pattern's low and a line minus a cushion are acceptable alternatives.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the day's low, then size from the stop.

wrong.At the low of the first pullback: That is a pattern low, an acceptable alternative. It can sit far from the entry, so the day's low comes first.
wrong.At the 50-day average: A line minus a cushion is an acceptable alternative. The day's low is the primary stop.
wrong.Exactly on the day's low: Our rule is a few cents under the low, not exactly on it.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under the day's low. The loss is then known before you buy, and the size comes from it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62) and the held decision D-008 on which low

questions.story: Bought on the breakout today. Look at today's bar and the bars before it.

questions.q: A tight base in a downtrend can still be a VCP.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A VCP is a pause inside an uptrend. Minervini goes long only in a Stage 2 uptrend and never goes against the long-term trend. A base in a downtrend is just a stock that is still falling. A close under the 200-day also ends our setup before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: The base sits inside an uptrend. A tight base in a downtrend does not qualify.
questions.simple: False. A VCP is a rest inside an uptrend, and a base in a downtrend is just a stock still falling.

reasons: rests on held decisions D-029 and D-060 (prior advance, trend template), kept out of the key

questions.q: Which trend does a VCP belong in?
choices: A Stage 2 uptrend
A Stage 4 downtrend
A sideways drift under the 200-day
questions.answer: A Stage 2 uptrend
questions.why: A Stage 2 uptrend. Minervini goes long a Stage 2 uptrend and never against the long-term trend.
questions.lesson_line: Long VCPs belong in uptrends. Check the trend before the box.

wrong.A Stage 4 downtrend: Minervini goes short a Stage 4 downtrend. A long VCP does not belong there.
wrong.A sideways drift under the 200-day: Below the 200-day we do not buy. The long needs a trend under it.

questions.q: The app's market filter (Green to Red, most open to most cautious) reads Red. A perfect VCP breakout is still a buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The market filter has four colors, Green to Red, and each says what the account may do. Red is the most cautious: we are mostly in cash, so we pass on VCP buys. ChartMill: in a negative market even perfect VCPs fail en masse, because there are not enough buyers to carry breakouts through.
questions.lesson_line: Red market: mostly cash, so we pass on VCP buys. Even perfect bases fail when buyers are missing.
questions.simple: False. Red means mostly cash, and even perfect VCPs fail when too few buyers are around.

deeper.counter: Red does not say the pattern is bad. It says the market cannot carry it. ChartMill: in a negative market, even perfect VCPs fail en masse. There are not enough buyers to carry breakouts through.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D46) and the card's market reading line

questions.q: What is the lowest RS rating we accept for a VCP leader?
choices: 80 or more
70 or more
90 or more
60 or more
questions.answer: 80 or more
questions.why: 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. The RS rating ranks a stock's strength against all other stocks. We buy leaders because a breakout needs buyers to carry it, and leaders have them. Minervini's own floor is 70, preferably in the 90s, and our line is stricter.
questions.lesson_line: We buy leaders: RS 80 or more in a strong group.

wrong.70 or more: That is Minervini's floor. Our line is higher.
wrong.90 or more: The 90s are Minervini's preference. We accept 80 or more.
wrong.60 or more: Too low for a leader. Our line is 80 or more, in a strong group.

questions.simple: We buy leaders, stocks with an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group. A breakout needs buyers behind it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C31), which beats Minervini's floor of 70

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We take no longs below the ___-day simple moving average.
questions.why: 200. We take no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. The card says the same: price above the 200-day SMA at the buy. A close under it ends the VCP idea before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: No longs under the 200-day. A VCP has to pass that first.
questions.simple: The 200-day average. We do not buy a long that sits below it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: If the pullbacks in a base stop shrinking, it is not a VCP.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A contraction as deep as, or deeper than, the one before ends the VCP idea. The contractions must shrink.
questions.lesson_line: No shrinking, no VCP. A wide and loose base waits.

questions.q: Which floor applies to a VCP we buy?
choices: $5 a share and $5 million a day
$10 a share and $20 million a day
No floor if the base is tight
$10 a share, with any dollar volume
questions.answer: $10 a share and $20 million a day
questions.why: $10 a share and $20 million a day. UCT trades only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Both tests apply. The floor is the same for every setup, however tight the chart.
questions.lesson_line: Thin, cheap stocks are off the list however tight the chart.

wrong.No floor if the base is tight: A tight chart on a thin stock is still a pass.
wrong.$10 a share, with any dollar volume: Both tests apply. The stock must also trade at least $20 million a day.

questions.simple: Trade only stocks that cost at least $10 and trade at least $20 million a day. A tight chart changes nothing.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (h09)
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: The first pullback is 24%. Each next one is half the last. How deep is the third?
questions.why: Halve the 24% once for the second pullback, then halve that result for the third, which gives 6%. Minervini likes each contraction to be about half of the one before, give or take. That is a rule of thumb, so real bases land near it, not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: About half each time. The swings shrink fast.
questions.simple: Halve the 24 percent once, then halve the result again. That leaves 6 percent for the third pullback.

deeper.example: Minervini's classic progression runs from a 25 percent correction to 10 percent to 5 percent. Those steps are not exact halves. His rule of thumb is about half, give or take. Use half as a guide, not a fixed ratio.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+2 sits beside the held decision D-059 on the contraction ratio
+1 fixed before

wrong.12%: That stops after one halving. It is the second pullback.
wrong.3%: That halves three times. The third pullback is two halvings in.
wrong.8%: That divides 24 by 3. Each pullback is half the last.

questions.lesson_line: Depth is high minus low, divided by the high. The last swing should be the tightest.
questions.simple: Take the high minus the low, then divide by the high. For 170.00 and 164.05 that is 3.5 percent.

wrong.6.0%: That is the dollar amount read as a percent. Divide it first.
wrong.96.5%: That is the low as a share of the high, not the drop.

questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent before you size the trade.
questions.simple: The stop is 2.7 percent under the fill. That is inside our usual range, and the size comes from the stop.

questions.simple: Two R is two gaps above the fill. There the stop may move to breakeven, so a winner cannot turn into a loser.

questions.q: The pivot is 16.47. The chase limit is 4% above it. What price is that, to the nearest cent?
questions.why: The chase limit is the pivot plus 4%. Multiply the pivot by 1.04: 16.47 times 1.04 is 17.13 to the nearest cent. Past it, the stop stays put, the distance grows and the shares shrink. ChartMill: buy at the line of least resistance, not three weeks after the breakout, when the price is already 20% higher.

questions.simple: Add 4 percent to the pivot to get 17.13. Past that the stop stays put, so the shares shrink and you are chasing.

deeper.trap: Do not mix up two limits. The chase limit is 4% above the buy point. The stretch limit is separate: skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA. A buy has to pass both.

choices: Buy half now and the rest on a dip
Buy it now; the volume is heavy
Pass; more than 4% past the pivot
Buy fewer shares; the risk is the same

questions.q: On this chart, the last swing of the base is its tightest.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The final swing meets the fewest sellers, so it is the smallest. ChartMill calls it the most important contraction and says it has to be tight. A tight last swing also keeps the stop close under the pivot, so the risk is small.
questions.lesson_line: The last swing is the tightest, and it sets the pivot.
questions.simple: True. The last swing meets the fewest sellers, so it is the smallest and keeps the stop close.

reasons: final contraction at most 10% is a proposed card criterion

questions.q: How should volume look in the final contraction?
choices: Drying up as the price tightens
Spiking on a wide, heavy down day
Rising above its usual level
The same as in the first swing
questions.answer: Drying up as the price tightens
questions.why: Volume dries up. In the final, tightest swing the sellers have run out, so few shares trade. ChartMill: the drying-up volume confirms there is no one left who wants to sell at these prices. Minervini ties shrinking swings to falling volume. On this chart the quiet days pile up into the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet price, quiet volume. Volume dries up into the tight final swing.

wrong.Spiking on a wide, heavy down day: That is the opposite of a dry-up. A heavy down day is a warning to note.
wrong.Rising above its usual level: Busy trading is not a dry-up. Quiet days are what show the sellers have gone.
wrong.The same as in the first swing: The first swing had the most selling. The last should be quieter.

questions.simple: Volume dries up as the price tightens, a sign the sellers have run out.

reasons: the specifics rest on one card line (c05)
volume_dry is a proposed criterion

questions.story: The day before a breakout. Look at the volume bars in the last swing.

questions.q: Is this base tightening the way a VCP should?
choices: No; the second swing barely shrank
Yes; the second swing is smaller
Yes; two swings are enough
No; the first swing is too shallow
questions.answer: No; the second swing barely shrank
questions.why: No. Minervini likes each contraction to be about half the one before. Here 9.0% is most of 11.5%, so the sellers have not thinned out. ChartMill: what matters is that the pullbacks contract. This base stayed wide and loose.
questions.lesson_line: Swings that barely shrink make a loose base, not a VCP.

wrong.Yes; the second swing is smaller: It is smaller, but barely. A VCP needs each swing clearly smaller than the last.
wrong.Yes; two swings are enough: Two swings can make a VCP, but only when the second is clearly smaller.
wrong.No; the first swing is too shallow: 11.5% is a normal first swing. The trouble is that the second barely shrank.

questions.story: The day before it trades through its pivot. The base has two pullbacks, 11.5% then 9.0%.
questions.simple: No. The second swing is nearly as big as the first, so the sellers have not thinned out.

reasons: wide-and-loose invalidation is a proposed card criterion
the story uses equal swings against a ratio that is a held decision (D-059)

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A VCP
A flat base
A high tight flag
A cup with handle
questions.answer: A flat base
questions.why: A flat base. One box where the swings stay the same size has no real volatility contraction. Minervini describes a flat base of four to seven weeks as a tight, narrow box. This one rests six weeks after a 40% run. A VCP's pullbacks shrink one after another, and this box has none that do.
questions.lesson_line: Same-size swings are a box. Shrinking swings are a VCP.

wrong.A VCP: A VCP needs successive pullbacks that shrink. These do not.
wrong.A high tight flag: A high tight flag follows a run of 90% or more in 8 weeks or less. This run was 40% over four months.
wrong.A cup with handle: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle at the rim. This is a flat box.

questions.story: After a 40% run over four months, a leader rests six weeks in a 10% range. The swings inside stay about the same size.
questions.simple: A flat base. The swings stay about the same size, so nothing is shrinking the way it does in a VCP.

deeper.counter: A tight box can still break out, and that does not turn it into a VCP. A flat base has no shrinking pullbacks and breaks out above the base high. A VCP is defined by the shrinking, not by the breakout.

reasons: +2 rests on the held decisions D-002, D-042 and D-043 (flat base against VCP, length and depth)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: By our rule, which base is the VCP?
choices: Base B; its pullbacks get smaller
Base A; one deep pullback is enough
Both; each pulls back and recovers
Neither; a VCP needs a cup shape first
questions.answer: Base B; its pullbacks get smaller
questions.why: Base B. A VCP strings pullbacks that shrink one after another, from greater volatility on the left to lesser on the right: 18%, 9%, 4%. Base A has one pullback, so nothing shrinks.
questions.lesson_line: A VCP is a string of shrinking pullbacks. One pullback is not a string.

wrong.Both; each pulls back and recovers: Every base pulls back. A VCP needs pullbacks that shrink one after another.
wrong.Base A; one deep pullback is enough: One pullback has nothing to shrink. A VCP needs a string of them.
wrong.Neither; a VCP needs a cup shape first: A cup is a different base: one rounded decline and one handle. A VCP is read by its shrinking pullbacks.

questions.story: Base A has one 15% pullback, then drifts up to the pivot. Base B has three pullbacks: 18%, 9% and 4%.
questions.simple: Base B is the VCP, because its three pullbacks keep shrinking, while Base A has only one pullback.

reasons: count questions sit near the held decision D-058 (contraction count), kept out of the key
key rests on one card line (c33) plus a general Minervini line

questions.q: Buy or pass?
choices: Buy with a wider stop
Pass; the base has broken
Buy; it cleared the pivot
Wait a day and buy at the open
questions.answer: Pass; the base has broken
questions.why: Pass. The entry day's low is already under the final contraction's low, so the base has broken and there is no trade. ChartMill: if price drops below that low, the final contraction has failed to hold and the premise of the trade is gone. Clearing the pivot is not enough, and a wider stop does not fix a broken base.
questions.lesson_line: The structure comes first. If the day's low breaks the last swing's low, there is no trade.

wrong.Buy; it cleared the pivot: Clearing the pivot is only half the test. The final low must hold.
wrong.Buy with a wider stop: Widening the stop is a named mistake. The structure failed.
wrong.Wait a day and buy at the open: Waiting a day does not repair a broken base. By our rule there is no trade.

questions.story: Price trades through the pivot at 11:00. The day's low so far is already under the final contraction's low.
questions.simple: Pass. The day's low is under the last swing's low, so the base has broken and a wider stop will not fix it.

reasons: +2 keys a proposed card check (vcp.stop_structure_check) beside the held decision D-008

questions.q: What now?
choices: Add more; it is cheaper
Sell it all at tomorrow's open
Hold; the stop is the exit
Widen the stop to give it room
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. A breakout day that closes back inside the base is the squat: sellers pushed the stock back, which is a warning. A warning is not proof, so the stop is still the exit, and it only moves up. We do not add either, since the plan is one full buy. In the real ALGN case the next day's low took the stop, a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: A squat is a warning. The stop decides the exit.

wrong.Add more; it is cheaper: We never add. One full buy, one stop.
wrong.Sell it all at tomorrow's open: A warning is not an exit. The stop decides.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never wider. Widening it to give the stock room is a named mistake.

questions.story: Bought the breakout at 28.65 with the stop at 27.70. It closes at 28.14, back inside the base, still above your stop.
questions.simple: Hold. A close back inside the base is a warning, but only the stop proves the trade wrong.

deeper.counter: A warning is not a shrug. In our scan of past VCP buys, a close back inside the base reached 3R about half as often as a close above the pivot. So the squat is a real warning, but the stop still decides the exit.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit) and a proposed card warning

questions.q: Buy the breakout today?
choices: No; wait until after the report
Yes, but only at half the size
Yes; the setup is a perfect one
No; drop it from the list for good
questions.answer: No; wait until after the report

questions.q: A close under the 20-day average soon after the breakout is a warning, not an exit.
questions.answer: True

questions.q: On this chart, what do the higher lows mean?
choices: It drifts under the first low
Each high is below the last
The last low is above the base low
Each pullback ends at one low
questions.answer: The last low is above the base low
questions.why: The last low is above the base low. Each dip ends at a higher price, so buyers step in sooner. Kullamagi, who never uses the word VCP, describes the same orderly look in his breakout setup: higher lows and a tightening range.
questions.lesson_line: The final low should sit above the base's lowest low.

wrong.It drifts under the first low: A low under the first low is the opposite of a higher low.
wrong.Each pullback ends at one low: Equal lows are a flat floor. The final low must sit above the base's lowest low.

reasons: key rests on one card line (c04)
the second source describes a different setup
higher_lows is a proposed criterion

questions.story: The day before a breakout. Compare the low of each swing.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A VCP in the making
A flat base after a rally
A high tight flag
A cup with a handle

questions.lesson_line: Measure the pole first. A near-double that pauses is a high tight flag.

wrong.A VCP in the making: A VCP shows pullbacks that shrink one after another. This is one quiet pause after a double.
wrong.A flat base after a rally: A run of 90% or more in 8 weeks or less, then a pause, is a high tight flag. It is not a flat base.
wrong.A cup with a handle: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle at the rim. This is a quick pause after a double.

questions.q: By our rule, which test fails?

The first pullback is too shallow
The last pullback is too wide
Nothing; 11.5% is about half of 24%

questions.lesson_line: The last swing has to be the tightest. 11.5% is still loose.

wrong.The first pullback is too deep: A 24% first leg is inside the 10% to 40% range. The last swing is the problem.

The pullbacks are not shrinking

A cup with handle
A textbook VCP

questions.q: A VCP trades through its pivot. Do you buy it?

Pass; the heavy day voids the setup
Wait until the next base forms
Buy it, but with a wider stop

wrong.Buy it, but with a wider stop: The stop never widens for a worry. It stays a few cents under the entry day's low.

questions.lesson_line: Light volume is a red flag. The stop is still the exit.

Between 2R and 5R
Between 5R and 8R
Between 8R and 10R
questions.answer: Between 2R and 5R
questions.why: Between 2R and 5R. Breakeven is the point after which a trade must never again become a loser, so we do it once the trade has earned it. ChartMill: management takes over with a rising stop and partial profits, and a winner must never turn into a loser. The stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven stop, ideally between 2R and 5R. The stop only moves up.

wrong.Between 5R and 8R: Ideally the move comes between 2R and 5R. Past 5R a stop still under the entry gives back too much.

wrong.Both are about equally clean: Both shrink, but Base B's second swing is still most of its first.

Raised after the breakout

questions.answer: False

questions.q: Which average is the default trail for a fast-moving VCP?

The 9 EMA
The 200-day
The 20 EMA
questions.answer: The 9 EMA
questions.why: The 9 EMA for a fast mover. A fast mover stays close to its 9 EMA, so a close below it says the run has changed. A steadier mover gets more room from the 20 EMA. We sell what is left on a close below the trail. The first sell comes earlier and is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover: trail the 9 EMA. Steadier: trail the 20 EMA.

Add more while it is quiet
Hold; the base was perfect
Move the stop to breakeven, hold

questions.lesson_line: A trade that does nothing for 10 days is sold.

wrong.Move the stop to breakeven, hold: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R, and this trade is up only 0.5R. A trade under 1R after 10 days is sold.

questions.q: What governs the exit?

Keep the old stop and wait it out
Wait for a recovery of the gap
Widen the stop to give the stock room

questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets the 30-minute rule. Past 2R, get out.

wrong.Wait for a recovery of the gap: The gap rule does not wait. It sets a new stop.
wrong.Keep the old stop and wait it out: The stock is already through it. The gap rule takes over.
wrong.Widen the stop to give the stock room: A stop only moves up. The gap rule is the one exception, and it sets the first 30-minute low, not a wider stop.

No difference between them
A close back inside the base
The day on the most volume

It lowers it; low broke
It voids the setup
No change; it is noise

Only A+ setups, no B grades
The A+ and the best B grade

Take it at half size, weak group
Take it; Minervini's floor is 70
Pass; the RS rating must be 90 or more

questions.q: What happens to the setup?

It is off; the trend test failed
It is off, only on heavy volume

wrong.It is fine; one close is noise: A close under the 200-day ends it before the buy.

questions.simple: The setup is off. A close under the 200-day means a downtrend, and we do not buy longs there.

deeper.trap: A tight base is not a trend. The base can look perfect while the trend test fails. The 200-day check comes first, and for a stock there is no way around it. Only indexes and leveraged ETFs may be bought under it, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long.

It still stands; buy through it
It moves down to the new low
The stock is banned for good

questions.lesson_line: Close under the last low and the count restarts.

wrong.It still stands; buy through it: The structure broke. The old pivot is gone.

wrong.The stock is banned for good: A new tight contraction can make a new pivot. The stock can set up again.

questions.simple: The old pivot is void. A close under the last swing's low means buyers failed, so wait for a new tight swing.

deeper.trap: The trap is waiting for the old pivot to come back. After a close under the final low, that pivot no longer matters. Watch for a new tight swing, then use its high as the new pivot.

questions.q: A stock down 70% from its high can still form a good VCP base.
questions.answer: False

questions.lesson_line: A stock that has fallen far is damaged, not resting. A VCP is a pause in an uptrend.
questions.simple: False. A VCP is a pause in an uptrend, and a stock that has fallen that far is damaged, not resting.

deeper.trap: The trap is a cheap-looking chart. A big fall can leave a tight-looking base, but the stock is no longer a leader pausing. The trend check and the leader rule usually catch it too.

questions.q: How big is the position?

2% of the account
40% of the account
1% of the account

questions.q: The day before a breakout. Which description fits the base?

Equal swings, steady volume
Widening swings, rising volume
One deep drop and a short handle

questions.why: Shrinking swings, and volume that dries up. RNG's contractions were 16.6%, 11.0% and 3.5%, and the final swing was quiet, on volume 0.46x the average. Few sellers were left, and it broke out the next day on 2.4x volume.

the bars were not checked by the writer

questions.q: Pullbacks shrink, 14% then 4%, but the last leg's volume stayed above average. What does that tell you?
choices: Supply may still be coming
Volume does not matter in a VCP
The base is done; buy at the pivot
The 4% leg is too deep
questions.answer: Supply may still be coming
questions.why: Supply may still be coming. Minervini ties shrinking swings to falling volume, and says that if volume does not quiet down on the right side, supply is likely still coming to market. Volume raises the grade rather than gating the setup. Our grade is a judgment of how clean a setup is. Here the final leg ran at 1.13x the 50-day average.
questions.lesson_line: Shrinking price is not enough. Volume should dry up in the last leg too.

wrong.Volume does not matter in a VCP: It matters. Falling volume shows the sellers are gone, and busy volume lowers the grade.
wrong.The base is done; buy at the pivot: A busy last leg is not a finished base. It shows less than a clean VCP does.
wrong.The 4% leg is too deep: 4% is a tight last swing. The trouble is the volume.

Check it, then set your own plan
Buy half and set a stop later
Wait for a second video to agree

Pass; Red means no VCP buys
Buy a starter

Base B: a quiet right side
Neither; volume does not matter

A tighter chase limit above the pivot
A looser stop on the entry day
Nothing; only the shape counts

Buy half now
Buy all now at a tight stop

Keep the stop and size to it
Pull the stop in to fit the size
Use a mental stop you can adjust

questions.q: What do you do with the position?
choices: Sell a big part into the strength
Add, since the leg is strong
Hold it all until trail breaks
Sell a small part, then hold
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the strength
questions.why: Sell a big part into the strength. A climax run packs a lot of gain into a few days, so it is the moment the position is worth the most. We sell a big part into it and trail the rest; how much is a judgment call. Adding is the opposite of our plan, which is one full buy with no adding.
questions.lesson_line: Into a climax run, sell a big part. How much is your call.

wrong.Add, since the leg is strong: No adds. A climax is where we sell, not where we buy more.
wrong.Hold it all until trail breaks: Our plan is to sell a big part into a climax, not to wait for the trail.
wrong.Sell a small part, then hold: A climax calls for a big part. How much is a judgment call, but a token trim leaves most of the position exposed.

questions.story: Your VCP winner is in a climax run: three gaps up in five days on rising volume, and a huge range today.
questions.simple: Sell a big part into the strength. A climax run packs a lot of gain into a few days, so we bank much of it.

deeper.trap: A strong leg feels like proof, so the pull is to add or to sit tight. Our plan for a climax run on your own long is to sell a big part into it; how much is your call.

questions.q: What is your move?
questions.story: A leader has RS 90, sits in a strong group and is above its 200-day. The app's market filter reads Green, which allows full risk. The final contraction is 4% deep. At 10:30 price trades through the 31.20 pivot, now 31.45, with the stop 2% under. It is 3% above its 9 EMA, and the report is 12 days away.
choices: Buy at market; stop under the low
Buy half now and half on a dip
Rest a limit at the pivot and wait
Pass; the report is too close
questions.answer: Buy at market; stop under the low
questions.simple: Buy at market, since a resting limit can miss the move, and put the stop a few cents under the day's low.
questions.why: Buy at market. Nothing in the story breaks a rule. RS 90 is over the 80 line, price is over the 200-day, and the stop is 2%, inside our 1-3% range. The report is 12 days away, outside the 3-day window. The stock is 3% above its 9 EMA, under the 10% skip line. Entries are market orders, because a resting limit can miss a breakout, and the stop goes a few cents under the day's low. We do not scale in.
questions.lesson_line: A clean setup is a market order with the stop a few cents under the low.

wrong.Buy half now and half on a dip: We do not scale in. One full buy, one stop.
wrong.Rest a limit at the pivot and wait: Our entries are market orders, not resting limits.
wrong.Pass; the report is too close: The rule bars new buys only in the 3 days before a report. This one is 12 days away.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 market orders, A3 stop, B22 earnings window)

questions.q: Buy the breakout through 42.00?
questions.story: A textbook VCP: shrinking pullbacks, a 5% final contraction, volume dried up. The stock trades through the 42.00 pivot at 42.15. Its 200-day line sits at 43.00.
choices: Pass; it is under the 200-day line
Pass; the final contraction is too wide
Buy; it is only a hair under the line
Buy half size until it clears the line
questions.answer: Pass; it is under the 200-day line
questions.why: Pass. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks, so a clean pattern does not rescue the buy. The 200-day sits at 43.00 and the stock trades at 42.15, under it. A stock under its 200-day is not in an uptrend, and Minervini never goes against the long-term trend. The exception is narrow: an index or a levered ETF, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: A clean pattern under the 200-day is still a pass. Wait for the line to be reclaimed.
questions.simple: Pass. Under its 200-day a stock is not in an uptrend, so we do not buy it, however clean the pattern looks.

wrong.Pass; the final contraction is too wide: The story calls it a textbook VCP with a tight 5% final contraction. The 200-day is what fails.
wrong.Buy; it is only a hair under the line: The rule is above the line at the buy. There is no allowance for being close.
wrong.Buy half size until it clears the line: The 200-day is a gate, not a size cue. Below it, we do not buy the stock at all.

questions.q: What do we usually do about the first sell?
questions.story: You bought a VCP breakout and the stop sits under the day's low. By the second day it is up 3R.
choices: Wait; day 3 or later, into a push
Sell a third now; 3R is the rule
Sell it all and bank the gain
Sell half now and add on a dip
questions.answer: Wait; day 3 or later, into a push
questions.why: Wait. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest, selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3-5 days, and says moves of 10-20x the risk are common in a bullish market. Winners pay for the small stopped losses, so we let them work.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment. We usually wait until day 3 and sell into a push.

wrong.Sell a third now; 3R is the rule: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R, and we very rarely sell on day 1.
wrong.Sell it all and bank the gain: That gives up the big winners that pay for the small losses. We sell part and trail the rest.
wrong.Sell half now and add on a dip: We do not add. One full buy, one stop.

questions.simple: Wait. Big winners pay for the small losses, so we rarely sell on day 1 and usually sell into a push from day 3.

reasons: D-013 (the first sell is a judgment, day 3 at the earliest, a 3, 5 or 7 day push); Kullamagi's 3-5 days and 10-20x risk quoted from his page

questions.q: Why does each smaller swing in a VCP matter?
choices: Fewer sellers are left each time
Buyers have lost interest
Volume is rising on each dip
The stock nears its 200-day
questions.answer: Fewer sellers are left each time
questions.why: Fewer sellers are left each time. Minervini: swings are biggest when sellers rush to take profits and shrink as sellers become scarcer. ChartMill says the same: each decline meets fewer sellers, so the pullback is shallower. That is why a tightening base is ready to break out.
questions.lesson_line: Each smaller swing means fewer sellers are left.

wrong.Buyers have lost interest: Smaller dips come when selling dries up, not when buyers leave.
wrong.Volume is rising on each dip: Volume dries up as the swings shrink.
wrong.The stock nears its 200-day: The swings say nothing about the 200-day. They show how much selling is left.

questions.simple: Each smaller dip means fewer sellers are left. That is why a tightening base is ready to move.

reasons: Minervini (his 2013 book, on his blog) and ChartMill's guide both give the sellers-scarcer reason, quoted word for word

questions.q: Do you buy it now?
questions.story: A leader is in the first big pullback of a base that may become a VCP, down 8% from its high. The chart looks cheap.
choices: No; wait for the pivot to trade
Yes; the first dip is the best price
Yes, but at half the size
No; the base needs two more months
questions.answer: No; wait for the pivot to trade
questions.why: No. The pivot is the line of least resistance, the place to get in. During the first pullback supply is still heavy, and ChartMill says not to buy then, nor three weeks after the breakout. For a VCP we buy as price trades through the pivot, not in the middle of the base.
questions.lesson_line: Do not buy mid-base. Buy as price trades through the pivot.

wrong.Yes; the first dip is the best price: A cheap-looking price mid-base is a guess. Supply is still heavy, and the pivot has not shown buyers are back.
wrong.Yes, but at half the size: We do not scale in. One full buy at the trigger, with one stop.
wrong.No; the base needs two more months: The wait is for the pivot to trade, not for a set number of months.

questions.simple: No. Mid-base the supply is still heavy, so we buy as price trades through the pivot, the line of least resistance.

reasons: Minervini's line of least resistance and ChartMill's not during the first pullback, both quoted word for word; the card names buying mid-base as a mistake

questions.q: Ten VCP buys at 0.5% risk. Seven stop out at -1R, one makes 8R, two make 2R each. What is the net?
questions.why: Seven stopped losses of 1R each are -7R. The 8R winner and two 2R winners add +12R. Net, -7 plus 12 is +5R, even though most of the buys failed. ChartMill: a failed breakout costs little because the stop is close, and a winner pays a multiple of that risk. Kullamagi says moves of 10-20x the risk are common in a bullish market.
questions.lesson_line: A few big winners pay for many small stopped losses.

wrong.+12R: That counts only the winners and forgets the seven losses.
wrong.+3R: That counts one 2R winner and the 8R winner against the losses, and misses the second 2R winner.

questions.simple: Add the winners and take off the losers. The small stopped losses are paid for by the few big winners.

reasons: ChartMill's worked example (its numbers) and Kullamagi's 10-20x quoted word for word; the arithmetic decides whether to accept small losses
